description: Looking at the blue sky is so commonplace that we forget to ask why. The answer lies in the light of the Sun and the air we pass through to see it.

hero.hook: The sky is not painted blue: it is a magic trick of light and air.

blocks.text: Looking up at the blue sky is so commonplace that we forget to ask why it is. The **atmosphere**, the layer of gas that surrounds the Earth, however, has no color of its own. This color comes from a very precise encounter between the light of the Sun and the gas molecules that float around us.

Understanding this blue means understanding how light travels and **dispersed**, that is to say, it returns in all directions instead of going straight. And nice surprise: it's exactly the same phenomenon that colors the sky red and orange at sunset.

Sunlight appears white to us, but it actually contains all the colors of the rainbow: it is [[visible spectrum of light]]. Each color corresponds to a **wavelength**, the size of its light “wave”. Blue and violet have short waves; red has long waves.
On the Moon, there is no air to scatter light. Result: there, the sky remains **black in broad daylight**, even when the Sun shines. Proof that the color of the sky comes from the air, not the Sun.

Because between the Sun and our eyes, the air is not empty: it is filled with tiny **gas molecules, especially nitrogen, approximately 78%** of the air, and oxygen, approximately **21%**. They are much smaller than light waves. When a ray hits them, it no longer goes straight: it is sent back in all directions. This little bounce is the starting point for the color of the sky.

In **1871**, the British physicist **Lord Rayleigh** put this phenomenon into an equation. He discovered that the shorter a color a color has, the more it is reflected in all directions by air molecules. It's the [[Rayleigh scattering]].
The sky of Mars is the opposite of ours: its iron-rich dust makes it pink during the day, but its sunsets are **blue**. It all depends on what the air contains.

blocks.caption: Blue light is scattered in all directions by air.

blocks.text: Concretely, blue light is scattered approximately **9 times more** than red. Red travels through the air almost in a straight line, while blue ricochets everywhere. This is why, wherever you look in the sky, blue always ends up reaching your eyes: the entire sky seems to “glow” with this scattered blue.
A logical question arises: if the shortest waves are the most dispersed, violet should win, because its wave is even shorter than that of blue. The sky also contains a lot of scattered purple.

The answer is not in the sky, but in our eye. We capture colors using sensors called **cones**, cells in the retina that are sensitive to light. They are much more sensitive to blue than purple. In addition, the Sun sends out more blue light than violet light. Our brain then does a sort of average and sees a beautiful blue. An animal sensitive to other colors would undoubtedly see a completely different sky.

The sunset follows the same rules, but changes one thing: the distance. At noon, light passes through a thin layer of air. In the evening, when the Sun is low, its rays must pass through **much more air** before reaching us.

blocks.caption: At horizon level, light passes through a much greater thickness of air.

blocks.text: On this long journey, all the blue is dispersed well before reaching us: it is filtered by the thickness of the air. Only the most resistant colors remain, reds and oranges. If there is dust or pollution, [[Mie diffusion]] comes into play: particles larger than air molecules make the sky milky or enhance these orange hues.
The sky is blue because short waves are about 9 times more dispersed by air than long waves. At sunset, light passes through so much air that only the red still reaches us.
